topic.name: Working with money
topic.description: Model real-world problems involving measurement, money, and time by choosing appropriate representations and interpreting results in context
evidence: Choose whether to use a bar model, number line, or equation for a measurement problem

topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} solves a real-life maths problem — like calculating how much fabric is needed for a project — can they choose the right representation (a diagram, a table, an equation) and explain what the answer means in the real situation?

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 modelling covers measurement, money and time, with multi-step problems and a choice of representation (bar model, number line, or equation), and the interpretation demand sharpens: the final answer must be read as the RIGHT quantity — 'is this the total cost or the change?' (CCSS MP4). Multi-step money is the signature context: a child must carry an interim result forward and then interpret the final number correctly. The persistent hazard remains suspension of sense-making (CDE) — computing to a number without asking whether it is reasonable or which quantity the question actually wants. Good teaching has the child choose and justify a representation, keep units throughout, interpret the final answer in context, and sense-check it; line plots from measurement data extend modelling to reading answers off a data display.
bestPractices: Have the child choose AND justify a representation for the problem (bar model / number line / equation), matching tool to structure (MP4 identify and map quantities)
For multi-step money, name each interim result ('that's the total cost') before the next step, and interpret the final answer as the quantity asked (change vs total)
Keep units attached throughout and sense-check the final answer against the situation (CDE)
Use line plots so children read answers off a data display back into the real-world question
Reason about the situation before computing; avoid reducing the problem to keywords (CDE)
keyRepresentations: Bar model for multi-step and comparison money/measurement problems
Number line for time and measurement jumps
Equation with units for total cost / change
Line plot of measurement data
commonMisconceptions: Reports the wrong quantity — gives the total cost when the question asks for the change
Stops after the first step of a multi-step problem
Computes without sense-checking whether the answer is reasonable in context
Drops or muddles units (mixing pounds and pence, or minutes and hours)

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, model real-world measurement, money, and time problems by choosing and justifying a representation (bar model, number line, or equation), carrying multi-step calculations with units attached, and crucially interpreting the final number as the RIGHT quantity (total cost vs change). The signature hazard is suspension of sense-making: computing to a number without naming which quantity the question asked for or checking its reasonableness. Line plots extend modelling to reading answers off a data display.

activities.title: Multi-step money modeller: name the quantity, then check it
feedback: When the child labels 85p as 'change', separate the quantities on the bar — the £1 whole, the 85p cost part, the change part — and label each, then ask which quantity the question wants
If the child stops at 85p, prompt: 'you found the cost — what does the question still want?'
If the child accepts 85p as change without checking, ask: 'could your change be 85p if you spent 85p from a pound?' to build the sense-check habit
Confirm when the child names 85p as cost, computes 15p change, attaches the unit, and checks that 85p + 15p makes the £1 paid
activities.rationale: Live build-and-check lets the child choose a representation, track interim results with units, and label the final number as the correct quantity with a reasonableness gate, directly targeting the interim-vs-final confusion. A linked bar panel that tracks the running parts with units and a prompt asking 'what is this number so far?' makes the interim-vs-final distinction concrete.
sourceClaims: MP4: identify important quantities and map their relationships with diagrams/tables/equations; interpret results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether they make sense.

Suspension of sense-making leads students to produce a number without checking realism; problem-specific supports that make students reason about the situation help, and reasoning about relationships should precede computing.
Bar models expose multi-step and comparison structure, helping children track which quantity is which through a problem.
learnerActions: Set up a shopping problem: two items at 65p and 20p, paying with £1
Choose a representation and say why it fits (e.g. a bar model with a £1 whole, an 85p part for the shopping, and a mystery part)
Pause at the interim number and label it: 'that 85p — what is it?' Answer: the total cost (65p + 20p = 85p)
Carry on to the second step: change £1 into 100p, then work out 100p − 85p = 15p as the change
Interpret the final number with its unit ('15p change') and sense-check it: the cost and the change together should make the £1 paid (85p + 15p = 100p = £1)
Transfer: re-run the model paying with £2 instead and describe what changes
activities.intendedInsight: In a multi-step problem each number along the way means something specific; the answer is only right when you name the quantity the question actually asked for and check it is reasonable in context.

activities.title: Shopkeeper who tries it on (spoken correction)
feedback: If the child accepts the shopkeeper's framing, ask them to point to where the cost ends and the change begins
Prompt the child to restate the final quantity with its unit and say how they know it is reasonable
This dialogue is never scored — treat it as thinking-out-loud practice
activities.rationale: Interpreting which quantity the answer is and reasoning about the situation is dialogic; a partner offering the total cost as if it were the change invites the child to reason about the relationships, sort out the quantities, and verbalise the distinction.
sourceClaims: Suspension of sense-making leads students to produce a number without checking realism; problem-specific supports that make students reason about the situation help, and reasoning about relationships should precede computing.
learnerActions: Play out a shop exchange where a shopkeeper rings up two items and states the subtotal as if it were the change
Catch and correct the error out loud, explaining which quantity the stated number actually is
Keep units straight (pounds and pence) while justifying the fix
Explain aloud how a bar or equation would separate the cost from the change
activities.intendedInsight: Distinguishing which quantity the answer names is a reasoning skill you can articulate and defend, not just compute.

activities.title: Worked multi-step walkthrough (scaffold)
feedback: After each revealed meaning, ask the child to predict what the next step computes and why
Prompt the child to restate which quantity is the final answer the question wanted
activities.rationale: A static worked example with revealable interim/final interpretations illustrates the process and the interim-vs-final distinction. As a scaffold it does not elicit the child's own representation choice or an independent sense-check, so pair it with a build-and-check task.
sourceClaims: MP4: identify important quantities and map their relationships with diagrams/tables/equations; interpret results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether they make sense.
learnerActions: Step through a worked multi-step money or measurement problem
Reveal what each step's number means (e.g. tap a step to show 'this is the total cost', 'this is the change')
Describe in your own words what the interim number means before seeing the next step
activities.intendedInsight: Each number in a worked solution carries a meaning; following the labels shows how an interim quantity differs from the final answer.

activities.title: Line plot from measurement data
feedback: If the child reads a value but doesn't tie it to the question, ask 'what does this number tell you about the objects you measured?'
Prompt a units and reasonableness check on the answer read from the plot
activities.rationale: Line plots extend modelling to reading answers off a data display and interpreting them in context, matching the measurement-data strand of the objective.

Create a line plot displaying the data
Use the plot to answer a real-world question, reading the answer off the display back into the situation
State what quantity your answer represents and whether it is reasonable
activities.intendedInsight: A data display is a representation you read answers from; the answer must be interpreted back into the real-world question with its units.

Have the child reason about the situation before computing; avoid reducing the problem to keywords

assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising 85p is the TOTAL COST (an interim quantity), computing the change as 100 − 85 = 15p, interpreting it as '15p change', and sense-checking that the change is less than the £1 paid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the wrong quantity: gives the total cost (85p) as if it were the change — confuses which quantity the question asks for.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the quantities on a bar (the £1 whole; the 85p cost part; the change part) and label each; reteach interpreting which quantity the answer names.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the change is 85p; treats the subtotal as the final answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after the first step: computes the total cost and doesn't carry on to the change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the step structure: 'you found the cost — what does the question still want?'; the child can do both steps but didn't monitor the goal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches 85 and stops, as if the problem is done; no second operation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspension of sense-making: doesn't check the final answer against the situation (change ought to be less than the £1 paid, and 85p change from spending 85p is suspicious).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'could your change be 85p if you spent 85p from a pound?'; build the habit of sense-checking against the context (CDE).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts 85p change without noticing it equals the spend and leaves nothing sensible; no reasonableness check.

responseLevels.gap: Gives 85 as the change; stops after one step and doesn't sense-check.
responseLevels.full: Names 85p as the total cost, computes 100 − 85 = 15p as the change, interprets it with its unit, and sense-checks it against the £1 paid — choosing/justifying a representation and transferring the interim-vs-final distinction to a new multi-step problem.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises 85 is the cost OR computes 15 as the change, but not both cleanly — e.g. finds 15 without naming 85 as the cost, or names the cost but doesn't finish/sense-check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a shop you buy two things: one costs 65p and one costs 20p. You pay with a £1 coin. A friend works it out and says 'the answer is 85'. Is 85 the change? Talk me through the problem — what does 85 mean, what is the change, and how do you know your change makes sense?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who models the multi-step situation and interprets quantities sees that 85 is the cost, not the change, and finishes the second step; a child who computes-and-stops offers 85 as the answer. The prompt separates them because 85 is a real, correct interim number — accepting it as the change reveals stopping early and confusing quantities, while rejecting it reveals full modelling. Hard to get right without carrying the situation through both steps.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Coin Values
topic.description: Recognise and know the value of different coins and notes
evidence: Identify 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2 coins
Know that a £2 coin is worth more than a 50p coin
Recognise £5 and £10 notes
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a handful of coins, can they name each one — like 2p, 5p, 20p — and sort them from least to most valuable?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to recognise each UK coin (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2) and note (£5, £10, £20, £50) and to know its VALUE — crucially, that a coin's value is a matter of convention, not its physical size, colour, or the number of coins. The central hurdle is that value is invisible: a small silver 5p is worth more than a larger bronze 2p, and one £2 coin is worth more than a heap of pennies. Learned through handling real money and repeatedly asking 'what is it WORTH?', not 'how big / how many?'.
bestPractices: Handle real coins and notes; sort and name them by value, not by appearance
Ask 'what is this worth?' and 'which is worth more?', separating value from size, colour and number
Contrast a small high-value coin with a large low-value one (5p vs 2p; £1 vs 2p)
Order coins by value along a value line (1p to £2)
Introduce notes once coins are secure; say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies (avoid 'a hundred times bigger', which invites size confusion)
keyRepresentations: Real coins and notes
Coins ordered on a value line (1p to £2)
A sorting mat by denomination
A 'worth' label held separate from the coin's appearance
commonMisconceptions: Judges value by physical size or colour (a 2p is bigger than a 5p, so 'worth more')
Thinks more coins means more money (a pile of pennies beats a single £2)
Confuses one penny and one pound
Doesn't recognise notes as money, or treats all notes as the same value

learn.summary: Young children (5-6) learn to recognise UK coins (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2) and notes (£5, £10, £20, £50) and to know each one's VALUE. The core hurdle is that value is invisible and set by convention, not by physical size, colour, or how many coins there are: a small silver 5p is worth more than a larger bronze 2p, and one £2 coin is worth more than a small heap of pennies (for example, ten 1p coins make only 10p). Activities centre on handling real money and repeatedly asking 'what is it WORTH?' rather than 'how big?' or 'how many?'.

activities.title: Till total: more coins is not always more money
feedback: If a child expects the heap of pennies to win 'because there are more', count the value of each set together: ten 1p = 10p versus one £2 = 200p, so fewer coins can be worth more.

If a child says the bigger 2p is worth more, ask 'what is it WORTH?' and point to the value shown on each coin (some designs show a number; others, such as the 2008–2022 shield designs, show the value only in words like 'TWO PENCE' and 'FIVE PENCE', so name the value for the child) — 5p is more than 2p, so the small 5p wins.
Reinforce by repeating the duel with different pairs (£1 vs 2p) so worth is separated from size and colour.
activities.rationale: Making the TOTAL VALUE visible and recomputing it as coins are added lets a child directly feel that value is independent of count and size, targeting the two central misconceptions (size/colour and more-coins-more-money). A running-total mat or till is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; real coins counted together serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y2 Money documents pupils counting the NUMBER of coins rather than their value ('Tiny has counted the number of £2 coins, not their value') and introduces the term 'worth'.
learnerActions: Drop real coins (or coins onto a running-total mat/till) one at a time and watch the TOTAL VALUE build up.
Drop ten 1p coins into the till and read the total (10p); then drop a single £2 coin beside them and see the total leap far higher than the whole heap of pennies.
Say in your own words why one coin can be worth more than many coins.
Run a 'which is worth more?' duel: put a big bronze 2p against a small silver 5p, predict which wins, then reveal/count the values to check.
activities.intendedInsight: A set's worth is its total VALUE, not the number of coins or their size; one high-value coin can outweigh many low-value coins, and the smaller coin can be worth more.

activities.title: Order coins on a value line
feedback: If a child orders by size, point to the printed value and re-place the coin by what it is WORTH.
Praise reasoning that cites the number/value on the coin rather than its appearance.
activities.rationale: Ordering by value along a line gives a durable mental sequence and repeatedly surfaces the small-coin-worth-more discriminator. Dragging coins onto a value line by worth (not size) is one concrete interactive form; a physical sorting mat and real coins work equally well.
learnerActions: Handle real coins and sort them, naming each by its value.
Place each coin in order from least worth to most worth along a value line running 1p to £2 (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2).
Notice where a physically small coin (5p) sits ahead of a physically bigger coin (2p) on the line.
Answer 'which is worth more?' for pairs you place, giving the value as your reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Coins have a fixed order BY VALUE that does not follow their physical size or colour; a 5p comes after a 2p even though it is smaller.

activities.title: Recognise and compare coins and notes
feedback: If a child confuses one penny and one pound, lay a real 1p and £1 side by side, name each, and say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies.
If a child treats all notes as the same, compare the printed values and ask which note is worth more.
When a child reads the number on a coin to decide, confirm that the number tells us what it is worth.
activities.rationale: Recognition is the stated curriculum objective and benefits from naming, value-recall and worth comparisons. A tap-to-reveal coin-and-note chart or lift-the-flap comparison is one supportive format; real coins and notes handled directly are the primary medium. Saying 'worth a hundred pennies' rather than 'a hundred times bigger' avoids inviting size confusion, per NCETM guidance.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'recognise and know the value of different denominations of coins and notes'.

NCETM guidance states 'Some children may confuse one pence and one pound' and advises 'It is helpful to avoid saying that one pound is one hundred times bigger than one penny as children may think this refer to the coin size rather than the value' — grounding the coin-value-independent-of-physical-size misconception.
learnerActions: Look at each coin and note and name it and say its value.
Reveal or state a comparison fact for each: 'is this worth more than, less than, or the same as a 10p?'
Introduce notes once coins are secure: name £5, £10, £20, £50 and say which is worth more.
Say that a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies (not 'a hundred times bigger').
activities.intendedInsight: Every coin and note can be recognised and matched to a known value, and notes are money too — different notes have different values.

activities.title: Shopkeeper: hand over coins by value
feedback: If a child hands over a coin chosen by size, ask them to read its value and pick again by worth.
Encourage answers that name the value rather than describe the colour or size.
activities.rationale: A role-play shopkeeper elicits recognition and value selection through talk and action and adds a purposeful context. This is a supporting activity: it is strongest when the child also physically handles and hands over real coins, so recognition is shown by doing, not only by speaking.
learnerActions: Play a shop where a shopkeeper asks you to hand over a coin by its value ('give me the one worth 5p', 'give me something worth more than a 10p').
Explain out loud why the coin you chose is worth what the shopkeeper asked.
Swap roles so you ask for coins by value too.
activities.intendedInsight: You can identify and select coins by their worth, using value rather than appearance to respond.

constraints: Use real coins and notes as the primary medium; interactive charts, tills and value lines are scaffolds that support, not replace, handling money.
Always ask 'what is it WORTH?' rather than 'how big?' or 'how many?', so value is held apart from size, colour and number.
Introduce notes only once coin recognition and value are secure.
Say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies; avoid 'a hundred times bigger', which invites size confusion.

A recognition matching/ordering/'which is worth more' task can check and reinforce value knowledge, but on its own it elicits selection rather than the child independently handling, totalling and explaining worth; pair it with hands-on comparison.
The shopkeeper talk activity supports recognition but should include physically handing over coins, not only naming them aloud.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (White Rose Y2 Money) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its 'counting number not value' example and the term 'worth' as unconfirmed, including where it is used as a sourceClaim on the till activity.

The original row claimed '3D adds nothing' for coin value. Coin value is indeed not a spatial concept, but this is a scoped observation, not an established universal law; a 3D/physical model could still support handling. Rephrased as medium guidance rather than a prohibition.

The original framed the till/value-line as the single format where the insight 'lands'. Retained as one concrete mechanism, not as the only way to teach it; counting real coins together serves the same purpose.

The Year 1 curriculum claim was left attached only to the recognition activity, where it directly matches the objective; it was removed from the value-line ordering activity's sourceClaims because it supports the general objective, not that specific method.

The assessment's ten-1p-vs-50p comparison was adapted to ten-1p-vs-£2 in the till activity (ten 1p = 10p vs one £2 = 200p); this is internally consistent and preserves the 'fewer coins can be worth more' principle, but differs from the original assessment numbers, which remain valid.

assess.poeTask: Put a heap of ten 1p coins next to a single 50p. Ask the child to PREDICT which is more money and, crucially, WHY, before anyone counts. Then count the value of the heap together (10p) against the 50p. A child who predicted the heap 'because there are more' meets the moment where fewer coins are worth more.
probeDeeper: 'This 5p is smaller than the 2p — so how can it be worth more?' (size vs value)
'You have more coins, but is it more money? Let's count what each pile is worth.'
'What does the number on the coin tell us?'
'If I gave you one £2 coin or five 20p coins, would you have the same amount? Which would you rather have?' (same value, different count)
assess.correctAnswer: Says the 5p is worth more than the 2p BECAUSE 5 is more than 2 (its value, not its size); says the single 50p is more money than ten pennies (50 > 10) despite fewer coins; says £2 > 50p and £10 > £5 by their values.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly — compare the printed values; handle a small high-value coin against a big low-value one repeatedly, always asking 'what does it say it is WORTH?'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the reason tier says the 2p is worth more 'because it is bigger'

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks more coins means more money — a pile of pennies beats a single higher-value coin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by counting the VALUE of each set (ten 1p = 10p vs 50p); show that one coin can be worth more than many.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ten 1p coins, because there are more of them
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the ten 1p coins over the 50p 'because there are more'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses one penny and one pound
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two explicitly with real coins; say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies rather than 'a hundred times bigger', which invites the size confusion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a 1p and a £1 as the same, or says £1 is 'one'

responseLevels.gap: Names some coins but judges 'worth more' by size, colour or number of coins; confuses penny and pound.
responseLevels.full: Recognises all coins and notes and compares them by VALUE, knowing value is independent of size, colour and number of coins (a small 5p beats a 2p; one 50p beats ten pennies; £2 > 50p).
responseLevels.partial: Recognises and names the coins/notes and reads their numbers, but is still caught when the smaller coin is worth more or a pile of small coins is set against one large-value coin.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the value, THEN the reason: (1) Show a 5p and a 2p: 'Which coin is worth more?' then 'How do you know?' (2) Show ten 1p coins beside one 50p: 'Which is more money?' then 'Why?' (3) 'Which is worth more, a £2 coin or a 50p coin? How do you know?' and 'Point to the £5 note and the £10 note — which is worth more?' Listen to the REASON: a correct child cites the printed value; an incorrect one cites size, colour or how many.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 5p-vs-2p item is the hinge: the smaller coin is worth more, so a child reasoning by size gives the wrong answer while a child reasoning by value gives the right one — hard to get right for the wrong reason. The ten-pennies-vs-50p item catches 'more coins = more money'.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Adding money and giving change
topic.description: Find different combinations of coins that equal the same amount of money
evidence: Show that 50p can be made with 2×20p + 1×10p, or 5×10p, or 1×50p
Systematically find multiple coin combinations for a given total
Explain why different coin sets give the same total
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make exactly 30p, can they find two or three different ways to do it using different combinations of coins?

pedagogy.summary: Children find different combinations of coins that make the same total — e.g. 50p as one 50p, or two 20p and a 10p, or five 10p. The valuable skill is doing this SYSTEMATICALLY (starting from the largest coin, or swapping one coin for equivalent smaller ones) rather than at random, and understanding that the sets are equal because their VALUES sum to the same total even though the coins differ. A key constraint: only real denominations exist — there is no 8p coin, but any total can be built from the coins that do exist.
bestPractices: Work with real coins; build one total several different ways
Model a systematic method: start with the largest coin, or swap a coin for equivalent smaller ones (50p to two 20p + 10p)
Ask 'can you find another way?' and record each combination in an organised list
Discuss why the sets are equal — the same total value, different coins
Reinforce that only real denominations exist (no 8p coin), but any total can be made from them
keyRepresentations: Real coins arranged into equal-value sets
A part-whole model (total = these coins / those coins)
An organised list or table of combinations
Swapping one coin for equivalent smaller coins
commonMisconceptions: Uses a non-existent coin (e.g. an '8p') to make a total
Finds combinations unsystematically, repeating some and missing others
Tracks the number of coins rather than their total value
Thinks a set with more coins must be worth more, so two ways can't be equal

learn.summary: Year 2 learners (ages 6-7) find different combinations of real coins that make the same total (e.g. 50p as one 50p, or two 20p + a 10p, or five 10p). The core skill is working SYSTEMATICALLY — starting from the largest coin, or swapping one coin for equivalent smaller ones — and understanding that different coin sets are equal because their VALUES sum to the same total, even though the coins differ. A key constraint: only real denominations exist (there is no 8p coin), but any total can be built from the coins that do exist.

activities.title: Build a target several ways with a live-updating total
feedback: If a learner grabs for a coin that doesn't exist (e.g. an '8p'), note that there is no such coin and ask which real coins could make that part of the total instead.

When a learner finds a new combination, ask 'Can you find another way?' and add it to the organised list. pedagogy.summary: Year 2 (age 6–7) money problems stay within a single unit (pence): totalling the cost of items, and — the demanding part — finding change and answering 'how much more do I need?'. The pedagogical key is that change is a DIFFERENCE, and young children find it far easier to reach a difference by COUNTING UP (the 'shopkeeper's method') with real coins than by counting back or by written take-away. Teaching should make change a practical, coin-in-hand act before it becomes an abstract subtraction.
bestPractices: Build change by counting UP from the price to the amount paid, using real or realistic coins so the coins themselves record each step (e.g. 35p → +5p = 40p → +10p = 50p; change 15p) — the DfE mental-calculation guidance calls this the shopkeeper's method and notes many children find counting up easier than counting back.
Model the same jumps on an empty number line so the change is seen as the TOTAL DISTANCE travelled (the sum of the jumps), not a point on the line.
Connect 'how much more do I need?' to the identical counting-up structure — it is the same gap read the other way — so children see missing-addend and change as one idea.
Keep amounts to manageable, 'friendly' values first (bridging one multiple of ten), then extend; use role-play shops so the procedure is rehearsed in a real context.
Press children to CHECK reasonableness — count the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid.

activities.title: Give change at a role-play market stall (count up with coins)

If one coin too many goes in, show the running total overshooting the amount paid (past 50p) and invite the child to remove a coin and recount up.
If the running total is still short, point to the remaining gap: 'Counting on from 35p you've reached 40p — how much more to reach 50p?'

Optional live supports that make the mechanism visible: a running-total bar that starts at the price (35p) and rises with each coin to the amount paid (50p), and an empty number line on which each jump (+5, +10) draws itself from 35 up to 50.
activities.rationale: Counting up from the smaller to the larger value ('shopkeeper's method') is an easier route to a difference for many young children than counting back, and coins give a concrete record of each step. Physically building the change makes 'change as difference' felt before it is written.

Change/difference is best found by counting UP from the smaller to the larger number ('shopkeeper's method'); many children find it easier to subtract by counting up than counting back, and coins provide a record of how the change was given (worked example: 27p, change from 50p = 3p + 20p = 23p).
learnerActions: Set up a shop: a toy priced 35p, a 50p coin to pay with, and a pot of mixed coins.
Count UP aloud from the price to the amount paid, placing a coin into a change tray at each step: '35… (put in a 5p) 40… (put in a 10p) 50'.
State the change as the coins you built: 'The change is 15p — a 10p and a 5p.'
Check by counting the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid (35p + 15p = 50p).
Repeat with other friendly prices (e.g. 45p paid with 50p gives 5p), then extend to the source worked example 27p paid with 50p, counting 27→30→50 to give 3p + 20p = 23p.
activities.intendedInsight: Change is the DISTANCE travelled from the price up to the amount paid — it is the total of the jumps you make when counting up (here 5p + 10p = 15p), not a take-away you have to work out on paper. The coins themselves record how the change was reached.

Running-total bars (anchored at the price), number-line jumps, and a change tray are optional supports to make the gap visible — offer them to illustrate the mechanism, not as mandatory steps.

reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: change 15p = 10p + 5p and 35p + 15p = 50p; worked example 27p→50p = 3p + 20p = 23p; 45p→50p = 5p; missing-addend 15p→20p = 5p; ten 1p = 10p < one 20p; 15p = 10p+5p = 5p+5p+5p = 10p+2p+2p+1p. All consistent.
The 27p→50p worked example crosses more than one ten boundary, so it is presented as an extension of the friendly single-ten cases rather than as itself a single-ten bridge.

Value/running-total distinction maintained in the first activity: change coins total 15p, whereas the running total counted on from the 35p price reaches 50p; no wording states the change coins 'add up to 50p'.

The source labelled a 3D shop rendering as adding 'handling friction' and a role-play conversation as unsuited; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than restated as universal limits. A spoken shopkeeper exchange could in fact narrate the counting-up steps.

One cited source (NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives / Subtraction as difference') is marked verified:false in the row; the principle it supports (difference under-recognised because 'take away' is over-emphasised) is retained only as rationale framing, not cited as established evidence.

The original 'adds price + amount paid (35 + 50)' and 'counts single pennies inaccurately' misconceptions are addressed indirectly rather than as standalone correctives; a future revision could add an explicit change-activity prompt contrasting adding with finding the gap.

probeDeeper: 'Show me how you know that's the right change — can you count it back onto the 35p to make 50p again?'
'You gave me these coins; is there a way to make the same change with fewer coins?'

'How is finding my change like working out how much MORE you need to buy the 20p toy?'

For the second: identifies the 5p shortfall by counting on from 15p to 20p. In both, the coins/steps show a DIFFERENCE being built, and the child can check by rebuilding the paid amount.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to value: line up the child's handful against a single 10p+5p and count both totals; show that ten 1p is worth less than one 20p. Rehearse making the SAME value with different coin combinations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives too many low-value coins for the change, or is satisfied by the NUMBER of coins rather than checking their total value against the 15p gap.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two numbers instead of finding the difference — computes 35 + 50 = 85 (or grabs 85p) because 'take away' is the only subtraction they recognise and change isn't seen as subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act it out as a shopkeeper: physically count coins UP from 35p into the customer's hand to 50p, and name the total handed over as the change. Contrast 'the shop keeps 35p, you get the rest' with adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Combines the price and the amount paid; hands over far too much, or writes 35+50.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counting up but losing the running total when bridging a ten — reaches 40p, then miscounts the second jump (e.g. calls the change 10p or 25p).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: record each jump on an empty number line so the two jumps (+5, +10) are visible and can be added deliberately; keep amounts bridging a single ten until secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts a correct counting-on path but the total of the jumps is wrong at the multiple-of-ten boundary.

responseLevels.gap: Grabs coins without matching value, adds the two amounts, or cannot establish the change; judges 'enough' by number of coins.
responseLevels.full: Reliably builds change by counting up from price to paid amount, solves the missing-addend 'how much more' by the same move, checks by rebuilding the paid amount, and transfers to a new price.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the change for the friendly case by counting up, but loses the total when bridging a ten, or can do the change but not the equivalent 'how much more do I need?', treating them as unrelated.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a toy labelled 35p and give the child a single 50p coin and a pot of mixed coins. Say: 'Buy the toy and give me the right change — use the coins to show me how you work it out.' Then set a second toy at 20p and say: 'You have 15p. How much more do you need to buy this one?' Watch HOW they work, not just the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands change as a difference counts UP from price to paid amount and the coins record the gap; a child who does not either adds 35+50, grabs a random fistful of coins judging 'enough' by how many, or counts back and loses the total. Correct reasoning yields 15p by a visible counting-on path; the wrong ideas each yield a different, diagnosable move.

constraints: At Year 2 the central rule is recording pounds and pence separately and never writing £ and p together. The White Rose scheme (verified:false in the row) suggests Year 2 avoids decimal notation and uses 'and' (£5 and 30p); treat that stricter 'no decimal' guidance as unverified and do NOT use it to reject £1.50.

Assess by listening for correct USE in context — avoid asking the child to define a symbol in the abstract, as stated in the source's assessment approach.
A static price-tag poster or tap-to-reveal image can label £ and p but does not let the child build amounts or use the symbols in context; treat it as a labelling scaffold, not the main task.

reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog claimed a 3D/spatial format 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'can't' teach use in context. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established findings; softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements. A static image can still teach labelling.

The White Rose Education scheme is marked verified:false in the row; its Year-2 'record pounds and pence separately, pence below 100p, use "and" not decimal' guidance is unverified and conflicts with the objective's listed correct form £1.50, so it is not applied as a hard constraint against £1.50.
The example 150p = £1 and 50p was checked for arithmetic consistency: 150 pence = £1 (100p) + 50p — correct. 75p = 50p + 20p + 5p is correct. '£1.50p' is correctly flagged as invalid notation.

pedagogy.summary: Year 3 (age 7–8) extends money problems to pounds AND pence together: totalling two or three priced items and giving change from a whole amount such as £5 or £10, and recording with £ and p notation (e.g. £3.47). The efficient route to change from a note is the counting-on / finding-the-difference strategy, not written column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is that £.p looks like two separate whole numbers: pupils must exchange 100p for £1 and treat the amount as one quantity. (Note: the statutory Y3 guidance records £ and p separately and defers formal decimal notation to Y4; this topic's evidence uses the £3.47 form, so teach the notation carefully alongside the pence-and-pounds meaning.)
bestPractices: Find change from £5/£10 by counting UP from the total spent to the note (e.g. spent £4.45 → +5p to £4.50 → +50p to £5.00; change 55p), shown on an empty number line — avoids error-prone column subtraction across zeros.
Establish 100p = £1 concretely and insist that £ and p are one quantity, not two whole numbers; exchange 100 pennies for a £1 coin so the equivalence is enacted.
Use the part–whole structure for multi-item change: total the items first (the parts), then the note is the whole and change is the missing part.
Model and contrast correct vs incorrect notation explicitly (£3.47, not £347, 3.47p or £3.47p); have pupils see, say and record amounts in more than one way.
Encourage estimation before calculating (≈£4.50 spent, so change is small) so unreasonable answers are caught, and read amounts in a place-value-honest way rather than as two separate numbers.
keyRepresentations: Empty number line for counting-on change from a note
Real coins/notes with 100p→£1 exchange
Part–whole (bar) model: note = total cost + change
Place-value columns (£ | tenths/10p | hundredths/1p) shown aligned by the decimal point
commonMisconceptions: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers (adds the pence column past 100 without exchanging, or writes £3.7 for £3 and 70p).
Notation errors — omits the decimal point, mixes units (£3.47p), or writes pence as if pounds.
Attempts change from £10 by column subtraction and makes 'take smaller from larger' / subtract-across-zeros errors instead of counting up.
'Most coins = most money' persists, and reading '£2.47' as 'two point forty-seven' reinforces the two-separate-numbers error.

learn.summary: Year 3 learners (age 7–8) total two or three items priced in pounds and pence, give change from a £5 or £10 note, and record amounts correctly (e.g. £3.47). The reliable route to change from a note is counting UP from the total spent to the note (finding the difference), not column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is treating £.p as two separate whole numbers ('string-length thinking'); learners must exchange 100p for £1 and treat each amount as one quantity. Note: the National Curriculum's non-statutory notes and guidance for Year 3 say pupils record £ and p separately, and formal decimal recording of money is introduced in Year 4, so teach the £3.47 form carefully alongside its pence-and-pounds meaning.

activities.title: Shop till: total, pay, and count change up
feedback: If pence are added past 100 without exchanging (e.g. £2.60 + £1.85 written as £3.145 or £3.45), stop and build the pence physically, exchange 100p for a £1 coin, then re-read the total as a single quantity (the correct total is £4.45).

If change is reached by column subtraction from £5.00/£10.00 and digits are taken the wrong way across the zeros (e.g. 00 − 47 giving £1.47 or £2.53), redirect to counting UP from the total to the note on a number line.
Check any change by counting it back onto the total: does it rebuild £5.00? If not, the jumps were wrong.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a total bar that sums items as they are added; a number line that draws each counting-on jump; a coin tray whose 100p visibly animates into one £1 coin. These are illustrative, not required — coins, a paper number line and spoken rehearsal achieve the same purposes.
activities.rationale: Counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note is an efficient change strategy that avoids subtract-across-zeros errors, and enacting 100p = £1 confronts the 'two separate whole numbers' misconception by making the exchange visible.
sourceClaims: Change is efficiently found by counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note (shopkeeper's method), avoiding column subtraction across zeros; many children count up more easily than they count back.

Children commonly treat pounds and pence (whole-number and decimal places) as two separate whole numbers rather than one decimal quantity ('string-length thinking'), partly because of whole-number language such as 'three pounds and seventy-six pence'; standard decimal vocal reading ('two point five four pounds') is recommended to counter this.

Year 3 pupils should add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts; non-statutory guidance says they record pounds and pence separately and that decimal recording of money is introduced formally in Year 4.
learnerActions: Choose two or three priced items (e.g. a £2.60 car and a £1.85 book) and total them, building the total step by step (£2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45).
Pay with a £5 note and work out the change by counting UP from the total to the note, drawing each jump on an empty number line: £4.45 → +5p → £4.50 → +50p → £5.00, so change is 55p.
Collect the change as actual coins into a tray; when the pennies/pence in the tray reach 100p, physically exchange them for a single £1 coin and re-read the amount as one quantity.
Repeat for a single £3.47 item paid with a £5 note: count up £3.47 → £3.50 → £4.00 → £5.00 = £1.53.

Record the change in £ and p notation (e.g. £0.55, 55p), then say the amount in a place-value-honest way suitable for Year 3 (e.g. 'fifty-five pence'); avoid reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds (e.g. 'three point forty-seven' for £3.47). Reading the digits separately ('nought point five five') is also acceptable and is the decimal reading the cited research recommends.
activities.intendedInsight: Change from a note is a short counting-on jump from the total to the note, and an amount in pounds and pence is ONE quantity because 100p exchanges for £1.

activities.title: Record it right: correct versus incorrect money notation
feedback: If a learner writes £347 for £3.47, ask how many whole pounds that would be and compare with the coins in the tray.
If a learner writes £0.55p (£ and p together) or 55p inside pounds as £55, show the correct form next to it and ask which matches the coins.

Reinforce place-value-honest readings ('fifty-five pence', 'three pounds forty-seven pence') and reject only the compound-whole reading of the pence, such as 'three point forty-seven', which treats the pence like a separate whole number. Reading the digits separately ('three point four seven') is not an error and is the reading the cited research recommends.
activities.rationale: Notation and place-value errors (omitted decimal point, mixed units) are specific and nameable, and contrasting correct with incorrect forms at the moment of writing targets them directly.
sourceClaims: £ and p should not be written together (e.g. not £1.00p); pupils commonly record money incorrectly by omitting the decimal point or mixing units.

learnerActions: For a given amount of coins in a tray, write the amount in £ and p and check it against the coins.
Compare correct and incorrect recordings side by side (e.g. £0.55 vs £0.55p vs £55) and decide which one matches the coins, explaining how you know.
Record the same amount in more than one correct way where sensible (e.g. 55p and £0.55) and explain they are equal.
Practise see–say–record: see the coins, say the amount place-value-honestly, then write it without ever joining £ and p (never £3.47p).
activities.intendedInsight: Money notation carries meaning: the decimal point separates pounds from pence, £ and p are never written together, and the written amount must match the value of the coins.

activities.title: Estimate first, then check for sense
feedback: If an answer is wildly off (e.g. a change of £4.53 from £5 after spending £4.45, when only about 55p is expected), prompt the estimate check: does this match 'the change should be small'?
If the counting-back check does not rebuild the note, the jumps or columns were wrong — redo by counting up.
activities.rationale: Pupils rarely estimate first and so lack a sense of a sensible answer; building in estimation and a counting-back check gives a self-correction routine.
sourceClaims: Pupils make take-smaller-from-larger and subtract-across-zeros errors (e.g. in £10.00 − amount) reflecting weak exchange/place value, and rarely estimate first so lack a sense of a sensible answer.

Change is efficiently found by counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note (shopkeeper's method), avoiding column subtraction across zeros; many children count up more easily than they count back.
learnerActions: Before calculating change, estimate: 'I spent about £4.50, so the change should be small.'
After finding change, compare it with the estimate and say whether the answer is reasonable.
Verify change by counting it back onto the total to rebuild the note.
When paying with a £10 note instead of £5, predict how the change will differ and decide whether counting up or column subtraction would be easier.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating before calculating catches unreasonable answers, and change from a note can always be checked by rebuilding the note.

activities.title: Quick checks on notation and reasonableness
feedback: For a wrong choice, point back to the coins or value the amount represents and ask which written form matches it.
Note: selecting a correct form checks notation and reasonableness but does not show the learner can carry out the counting-on process — pair it with the hands-on till activity.
activities.rationale: Short recognition checks are well suited to the crisply testable notation misconception and to reasonableness, as a companion to hands-on calculation rather than a replacement; recognition alone does not elicit the production of the counting-on method.

learnerActions: Fill in the blank to record a shown amount in correct £ and p notation.
Choose which of several written forms correctly records a given amount (e.g. £3.47 among £347 and £3.47p, with the incorrect forms clearly present only as non-examples to be rejected).
Choose or state the correct change for a simple purchase from a note.
Put a set of money amounts in order from least to most to practise treating each as one quantity.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct notation and reasonable amounts can be recognised and chosen reliably once the single-quantity meaning is understood.

activities.title: Shopkeeper role-play to narrate the method (optional support)
feedback: Use this to rehearse and explain reasoning; it narrates the method but does not by itself give calculation practice with feedback, so follow it with actual totalling, change-finding and recording.
activities.rationale: Talking through the shopkeeper's counting-on method may support articulation of the strategy, but giving change is procedural and needs practice with feedback, which narration alone does not supply; the articulation benefit is a proposed, untested affordance.
learnerActions: Take the role of shopkeeper and, out loud, talk a 'customer' through giving change: name the total, then count up from the total to the note coin by coin.
Explain aloud why 100p becomes £1 while handing over the change.

constraints: Treat each money amount as ONE quantity: insist on exchanging 100p for £1, never carrying pence past 99 without exchanging and never writing three digits after the point.

Teach change from a £5/£10 note primarily by counting UP (finding the difference) on a number line; reserve column subtraction for cases without the across-zeros trap and only when done correctly with exchange.
Never present an incorrect money form (£347, £3.47p, £0.55p, pence written as pounds) as a correct option in a learner task; use such forms only as clearly labelled non-examples to be rejected.

Read amounts place-value-honestly for Year 3 ('three pounds and forty-seven pence', 'fifty-five pence'); the pitfall to avoid is reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds ('three point forty-seven'). Digit-by-digit decimal reading ('three point four seven') is acceptable and is the reading the cited research recommends.
Recognition/selection checks confirm notation and reasonableness but do not elicit the independent counting-on calculation; pair them with hands-on totalling, change-finding and recording.

The National Curriculum's non-statutory Year 3 notes and guidance say pupils record pounds and pence separately, with formal decimal recording of money introduced in Year 4; introduce the £3.47 form deliberately alongside its meaning, and expect some learners to still record pounds and pence separately.

The source worked example £5.00 − £3.47 = £1.53 is arithmetically correct (count up: £3.47→£3.50 is 3p, →£4.00 is 50p, →£5.00 is £1, total £1.53); retained as stated. £2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45 is also correct.
The misconception examples '£3.145/£3.45', '£2.53' and '£1.47' are deliberately WRONG forms shown only as error patterns, never as correct answers.

The Year-3-appropriate reading remains 'fifty-five pence'/'three pounds and forty-seven pence', with digit-by-digit decimal reading flagged as acceptable rather than wrong. The shopkeeper role-play activity had its sourceClaims set to [] because the attached counting-up claim supports only the method content, not the untested principle that verbalisation/role-play aids consolidation; the benefit is stated as proposed/may.

One cited source (NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives') is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about take-smaller-from-larger, subtract-across-zeros and lack of estimation is used to inform feedback but should be treated with that lower confidence.

pedagogy.summary: Children solve word problems about collections of US coins and bills — finding the total value, making change, and writing amounts with the $ and ¢ symbols appropriately. The deep difficulty is that a coin's value is ABSTRACT and matches neither its physical size nor the number of coins: a dime is smaller than a nickel yet worth more, and three dimes beat five pennies. Money is best taught as a MEASURE of value (like length or weight), using proportional manipulatives that make each coin's worth visible, introducing coins two denominations at a time to limit switches of counting pattern, and first building the skip-counting and place-value number sense that totalling coins depends on.

Build the underlying number sense first — skip-counting by 5s, 10s, 25s and place value — since totalling mixed coins is a skip-count-and-switch task
Teach 'counting on' from the largest coin; model correct $ and ¢ notation and when each is used (100¢ = $1)

activities.title: Proportional-coin workbench: build value and make change
feedback: When a learner picks the bigger or more-numerous set as worth more, lay each coin over its unit-squares so the 10 squares of the dime stand beside the 5 of the nickel — let the squares, not the coin size, settle it.
If a learner counts every coin by ones (2 dimes + 3 pennies = '5'), highlight that one dime is already 10 squares; start from a single denomination before mixing.
When a learner stalls switching from 25s to 10s to 1s (counts 25, 50, 75 then says '76' for a dime), model counting on from the largest coin and track the running total on a number line.
For a correct total reached by counting on, ask them to remake the same amount with different coins to confirm value, not a fixed coin set, is what matters.
activities.rationale: Fanelli & Tracy report that children equate value with size and that coins are not concrete representations of their own value, recommending proportional manipulatives over realistic play coins and teaching money as a measure of value. A running total that accumulates by value supports 'counting on' and switching counting patterns, which Chandler & Kamii link to the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones when making change (that source is marked unverified in the row). The side-by-side square comparison is a proposed way to target the size/number heuristics through what the learner sees and does.

pedagogy.summary: Year 4 (age 8–9) draws the measures strands together: pupils ESTIMATE, COMPARE and CALCULATE across different measures — length, mass, capacity and money in pounds and pence. Three distinct skills sit here. Estimation means producing a reasoned rough value (and using it to sense-check exact work). Comparison across units requires converting to a common unit first (1.5 kg vs 1200 g → 1500 g > 1200 g). Calculation with money now uses decimal £.p as one quantity. The recurring hazard across all three is treating a measure as two separate whole numbers (2 m 30 cm, £3.47) or comparing raw digits while ignoring units.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a deliberate step BEFORE exact calculation — round each price/measure to something friendly (£2.45 ≈ £2, 1.30 ≈ £1), get an approximate total, then compute exactly and CHECK the exact answer against the estimate.
For comparison, always convert to a common unit first and make the conversion explicit (1.5 kg = 1500 g); use double number lines or a bar to show why the digits alone can't be compared.
Use benchmarks/referents for estimation (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle, a £1 coin) so estimates are anchored, not guessed.
Handle money totals as single decimal quantities, aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1; connect £.p place value to metric decimals (2.30 m, £2.30).
Make 'is this answer reasonable?' a routine — an unreasonable exact answer signals an error to find.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark referents (metre stick, 1 kg mass, 1 litre, £1 coin) for anchoring estimates
Double number line / bar model for comparing across units
Place-value columns aligned by the decimal point (metric measures and money)
Rounding number line for estimation before exact calculation

Rounds after calculating rather than before, or rounds the wrong way, so the estimate is useless as a check.

learn.summary: Year 4 (age 8–9) learners estimate, compare and calculate across measures — length, mass, capacity and money in pounds and pence. Three distinct skills sit together: estimation (producing a reasoned rough value and using it to sense-check exact work), comparison across units (converting to a common unit first, e.g. 1.5 kg = 1500 g > 1200 g), and calculation with money as a single decimal £.p quantity. The recurring hazard across all three is treating a measure as two separate whole numbers (2 m 30 cm, £3.47) or comparing raw digits while ignoring units.

activities.title: Measure bench: estimate first, then check
feedback: If the learner skips the estimate and goes straight to an exact total: ask 'Before you worked it out exactly, what did you EXPECT the answer to be about — and does your exact answer match that?' Build the habit of rounding and adding for a ballpark first.

If an out-of-range exact answer is accepted without comment (e.g. £45 or £0.45 for the three items): point back to the estimate of about £4 and ask whether the result is plausible, then help locate the error.
If rounding happens after calculating or the wrong way, so the estimate cannot act as a check: practise rounding each amount before computing and comparing the two.
activities.rationale: Research cited here (NCETM, unverified in this row) suggests learners often skip estimating before calculating and so may lack a sense of a sensible answer, leaving errors undetected; committing the estimate before the exact value is revealed is intended to make reasonableness-checking a routine. A live estimate→reveal→gap loop (committing an estimate, then revealing the exact value and showing the error) is a proposed way to make the check concrete, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils rarely estimate before calculating and so lack a sense of a sensible answer, leaving errors undetected.
learnerActions: Face a task: three priced items (£2.45, £1.30, £0.75) to total, or two measures to compare.

Round each amount to something friendly (£2.45≈£2, £1.30≈£1, £0.75≈£1) and commit a rough estimate BEFORE seeing any exact answer — for example drag a slider or write the estimate down and lock it in.
Keep benchmark referents in view while estimating (a £1 coin, a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle) so the estimate is anchored rather than guessed.
Only after the estimate is committed, reveal/compute the exact total (£4.50) and look at the gap between estimate and truth.
Decide out loud whether the exact answer is reasonable: does it land near the estimate (about £4)? If not, treat that as a flag to find an error.
activities.intendedInsight: An exact answer that lands far from a sensible estimate signals a likely error; landing near it makes the answer plausible, though it cannot catch every small slip (e.g. £4.40 instead of £4.50). Estimation is a deliberate step before calculation and a checkable habit afterwards, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Convert before you compare: the balance that tips
feedback: If the learner picks the larger NUMBER regardless of unit ('1200 g is heavier because 1200 > 1.5'): ask 'What is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?' and make converting to a common unit the first step every time.
Offer the counterexample 'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' to show they are equal once converted.
If conversion is shaky, rehearse on a double number line or balance that you can only compare like with like.
activities.rationale: Comparison across units requires converting to a common unit first; making the conversion explicit (and, optionally, physically felt on a balance or number line) targets the digits-only misconception. A 3D balance or filling a container can add physicality to mass/capacity work, though the core reasoning is numeric rather than inherently spatial.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should estimate, compare and calculate different measures, including money in pounds and pence; non-statutory guidance says they build on place value and decimal notation to record metric measures including money, and use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units.
learnerActions: Take two measures in different units, e.g. 1.5 kg and 1200 g.
Before deciding which is larger, convert both to a common unit: 1.5 kg = 1500 g (using multiplication by 1000 from larger to smaller unit), or convert 1200 g = 1.2 kg.
Compare only once the units match: 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is heavier.

Optionally use a double number line or bar model to show why the raw digits (1.5 vs 1200) cannot be compared directly; a balance-scale tool that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips against 1200 g lets the comparison be seen rather than asserted.
Order a short set across units, e.g. 1.5 kg / 1200 g / 900 g, after converting all to grams (1500 g, 1200 g, 900 g).
activities.intendedInsight: To compare two measures reliably, first express them in the same unit; comparing the raw digits while ignoring the units can give the wrong answer (1200 > 1.5, yet 1200 g < 1.5 kg).

activities.title: Money as one quantity: totalling £.p
feedback: If the total has three digits after the point, or pounds and pence are added independently, or amounts are not lined up by the decimal point: return to £.p as one quantity, realign by the decimal point and exchange 100p for £1.
Connect back to metric decimals (2.30 m) so the same place-value reasoning transfers across measures.
Self-check the three items: pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50, pounds 2+1+0 = £3, giving £4.50 — use this to confirm the total.
activities.rationale: The 'two separate whole numbers' error affects measurement as well as money (using '2 m and 30 cm' as two whole numbers instead of 230 cm), driven by whole-number language; competence with two-place money amounts does not guarantee wider decimal understanding, so handling money as a single aligned decimal quantity is deliberately taught.
sourceClaims: The 'two separate whole numbers' error affects measurement as well as money — e.g. using '2 m and 30 cm' as two whole numbers instead of 230 cm — driven by whole-number language; competence with two-place money amounts does not guarantee wider decimal understanding.
learnerActions: Total three amounts such as £2.45, £1.30 and £0.75.
Treat each amount as a single decimal quantity, not as two separate whole numbers; align the amounts by the decimal point.
Add, exchanging 100p for £1 where the pence exceed 99, to get £4.50.
Check the result reads place-value-honestly: two digits after the point, not three (£3.150 would signal pence added past 100 without exchanging).
Connect £.p place value to metric decimals written the same way, e.g. 2.30 m alongside £2.30.
activities.intendedInsight: Money totals are single decimal quantities: aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1 avoids 'string-length thinking' that adds pounds and pence as independent whole-number columns.

activities.title: Benchmark estimation across length, mass and capacity
feedback: Ask 'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?' to surface whether the estimate is anchored.
If an estimate seems arbitrary, point to a concrete referent (metre stick, 1 kg bag, 1-litre bottle, £1 coin) and re-anchor.
Prompt transfer: having estimated a length, ask the learner to use the same rounding-then-check move on a money total or a mass.
activities.rationale: The DfE programme of study expects pupils to estimate across different measures and to transfer the routine between measure types; anchoring estimates to physical benchmarks/referents is a pedagogy-level recommendation (from the row's best practice) rather than a directly cited finding, so it is offered as a reasoned proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should estimate, compare and calculate different measures, including money in pounds and pence; non-statutory guidance says they build on place value and decimal notation to record metric measures including money, and use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units.
learnerActions: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres before measuring, stating what referent you used (a metre stick, a stride).
Estimate a mass against a known 1 kg bag, or a capacity against a 1-litre bottle.
Say the estimate aloud and the reasoning behind it, then measure or compute the exact value and compare.
Transfer the estimate→convert→calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money rather than only within one measure type.
activities.intendedInsight: Good estimates come from anchoring to physical benchmarks you know, and the same estimate-then-check routine works across every measure.

constraints: Estimation must be committed BEFORE the exact value is revealed or calculated — otherwise it cannot serve as a check and becomes an afterthought.

A labelled picture or benchmark image can show what a metre, 1 kg or £1 looks like, but on its own cannot run the estimate-then-check loop or a unit conversion; use it as a referent, not as the full activity.

Recognition/ordering formats (choose-the-heavier, order these) can rehearse and check each skill crisply but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own free reasoning; pair them with prompts asking the learner to state and justify the estimate and the conversion.

A 3D balance or container adds physicality to mass/capacity comparison but is optional; the core reasoning (convert, compare, estimate) is numeric and not inherently spatial, and is not needed for money or estimation.

Interaction examples (slider to commit an estimate, a balance that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips, double number lines, decimal-aligned place-value columns) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory tools.

Role-play dialogue does not by itself require the learner to carry out the estimation or unit conversion this objective targets, so on its own it may not elicit the procedural steps; if used, direct it to prompt the learner to state and justify an estimate rather than relying on it to teach the procedure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic self-check: £2.45 + £1.30 + £0.75 = £4.50 (pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50; pounds 2+1+0 = £3). This confirms the stated exact total.
Unit check: 1.5 kg = 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is correctly the heavier mass; the digits-only reading (1.5 < 1200) is the misconception, not a valid comparison.

One source (NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives') is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about learners rarely estimating is retained but treated as unverified, and the rationale wording was softened accordingly. Treating estimation-before-calculation as a habit is pedagogically reasonable but its efficacy is not independently established here.
Benchmark anchoring of estimates is drawn from the row's best-practice/pedagogy notes rather than from a directly cited source claim; it is retained as a reasoned recommendation.

The original framing that a live 2D interaction is 'exactly' the ideal and static/dialogue formats are 'poor' reflects a catalog preference, not established comparative efficacy; retained as design suggestions with stated affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

probeDeeper: 'Before you worked it out exactly, what did you EXPECT the answer to be about — and does your exact answer match that?'
'You said 1200 g is heavier — what is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?'
'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' (counterexample: equal once converted).
'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?'
assess.correctAnswer: Gives a reasoned estimate first (≈£2 + £1 + £1 = £4, or 'about £4.50') THEN the exact £4.50, and uses the estimate to check it. For the masses: 1.5 kg is heavier because 1.5 kg = 1500 g, which is more than 1200 g — stated by converting to a common unit, not by comparing 1.5 with 1200.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares across units by the digits, ignoring the unit — 'the 1200 g is heavier because 1200 is bigger than 1.5' (or bigger than 15).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make units common first, every time: convert 1.5 kg → 1500 g (or 1200 g → 1.2 kg) on a double number line or balance, then compare; rehearse that you can only compare like with like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the item with the larger NUMBER regardless of unit; does not convert 1.5 kg to 1500 g before deciding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Skips estimation and cannot judge reasonableness — goes straight to an exact calculation, produces an unreasonable total (e.g. £45 or £0.45 for the three items) and doesn't notice it's wrong.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: build the habit of rounding each amount and adding for a ballpark BEFORE calculating, then checking the exact answer against it — an exact answer far from the estimate flags an error to find.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No rough answer offered before calculating; an out-of-range exact answer accepted without comment.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'String-length thinking' in the money total — treats £2.45, £1.30, £0.75 as separate whole-number columns, adding pence past 100 without exchanging (e.g. £3.150) or misaligning the decimal points.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to £.p as one quantity: align by the decimal point, exchange 100p for £1, and read the total place-value-honestly; connect to metric decimals (2.30 m).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A total with three digits after the point, or pounds and pence added independently, or amounts not lined up by the decimal point.

responseLevels.gap: Compares raw numbers ignoring units, offers no estimate, and cannot total £.p reliably; accepts unreasonable answers.
responseLevels.full: Estimates before calculating and uses the estimate to check; converts to a common unit before comparing; totals money as a single quantity; and transfers the estimate–convert–calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates exactly and/or converts for a friendly case, but does not estimate to check, or can compare only when the units already match — lists results without judging reasonableness or transferring across measure types.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three price tags in front of the child — £2.45, £1.30, £0.75 — and say: 'First tell me ROUGHLY what these cost altogether, then work out the exact total.' Then show a 1.5 kg bag and a 1200 g bag and ask: 'Which is heavier — and how do you know?' Watch whether they estimate before calculating, and whether they convert before comparing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the idea estimates first (rounding sensibly) and converts to a common unit before comparing, so 1.5 kg is correctly heavier; a child who lacks it dives straight to an exact calculation with no reasonableness check, and/or judges 1200 g heavier because 1200 > 1.5 (or > 15). Estimating-before and converting-before each produce a visibly different move from the wrong ideas.
